question: What is the momentum p, of an object of mass m, moving with a velocity ?
solution:
The correct answer is __**p = mv**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Momentum is a fundamental concept in physics, defined as the product of an object's mass and its velocity.
 
• The formula for momentum (p) is given by p = mv, where m is the mass of the object and v is its velocity.
 
• Momentum is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction, aligning with the direction of the object's velocity.
 
• In classical mechanics, the conservation of momentum is a crucial principle, stating that the total momentum of a closed system remains constant if no external forces act on it.
 
• The SI unit of momentum is kilogram meter per second (kg·m/s).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Impulse:**

 
 
• Impulse is the change in momentum of an object when a force is applied over a time interval.
 
• It is calculated as the product of the force (F) and the time (∆t) during which the force acts, given by Impulse = F∆t.
 
• Impulse has the same unit as momentum (kg·m/s) and is also a vector quantity.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Second Law:**
 
 
• Newton's Second Law of Motion states that the force acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of its momentum, F = dp/dt.
 
• This law forms the basis for the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration.
 
 
 
• **Conservation of Momentum:**
 
 
• The principle of conservation of momentum states that in a closed system with no external forces, the total momentum before and after an event remains constant.
 
• This principle is widely used in collision and explosion problems in physics.
 
 
 
• **Elastic and Inelastic Collisions:**
 
 
• In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
 
• In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not; some of the kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy, such as heat or sound.
